_comment: Birding mnemonics + ID notes shown in the Bird Reference. Keyed by 4-letter species code. mnemonic = the catchy phrase birders use; id_note = how to tell it apart from look/sound-alikes. Independent of CSV-generated species.json, so it survives taxonomy regeneration. Expand freely.

NOCA.id_note: Clear, loud, down-slurred whistles that carry a long way; also a sharp metallic 'chip.' Both sexes sing.

CARW.id_note: Rich, rolling 'teakettle' phrase, astonishingly loud for such a small bird; also a dry, descending chatter.

BLJA.id_note: Harsh, slurred screams plus a musical 'queedle' pump-handle note — and a convincing Red-shouldered Hawk imitation that fools everyone.

AMCR.id_note: Familiar flat 'caw.' Compare Fish Crow, whose call is nasal and two-parted — 'uh-uh,' as if saying no.

TUTI.id_note: Clear, whistled 'peter' repeated 3-8 times; also scratchy, scolding chickadee-like notes.

AMRO.id_note: Liquid caroling of rising and falling phrases; sharp 'tut-tut-tut' alarm and a high, thin 'seee' flight note.

WTSP.id_note: Pure, plaintive whistles on a steady or slightly shifting pitch. Cleaner and sadder than the buzzy, jumbled Song Sparrow.

SOSP.id_note: Two or three clear notes, then a jumble that drops into a trill. Highly variable, but that 'few sweet notes then a buzz' shape is the giveaway.

CHSP.mnemonic: a dry mechanical trill, all one pitch
CHSP.id_note: Long, flat, mechanical trill like a sewing machine. Drier and faster than Swamp Sparrow; doesn't accelerate like Field Sparrow.

SWSP.id_note: Loose, rich trill — slower and far more musical than Chipping Sparrow's dry rattle. Favors wet, marshy edges.

SASP.id_note: Thin, buzzy, insect-like: a few sharp ticks then two buzzes, the second lower. Sounds more like a grasshopper than a sparrow.

FISP.mnemonic: a bouncing ping-pong ball coming to rest
FISP.id_note: Sweet, downslurred whistles that accelerate into a trill — like a dropped ball speeding up as it settles. Unmistakable once learned.

LISP.id_note: Rich and bubbling, recalling a House Wren or Purple Finch; rises then falls. Skulky bird — you'll hear it before you see it.

DOWO.mnemonic: pik!  ...and a whinny that falls down a hill
DOWO.id_note: Soft, high 'pik'; the whinny clearly descends in pitch. Smaller bill than Hairy. Compare Hairy's louder 'peek' and level rattle.

HAWO.id_note: Louder, sharper, lower 'peek!' than Downy; the rattle stays level instead of falling. Bill looks as long as the head is deep.

RBWO.id_note: Rolling, throaty 'churr' or 'kwirr'; also a laughing 'cha-cha-cha.' Named for a faint red belly you'll rarely see.

PIWO.id_note: Loud, ringing series that rises and falls irregularly — wilder and deeper than a Flicker. Slow, resonant drum that trails off at the end.

YBSA.mnemonic: a cat-like mew, then a stuttering Morse-code drum
YBSA.id_note: Nasal, cat-like 'mew' or 'queah'; the drum is irregular — a few quick taps then slowing, unlike any other woodpecker's even roll.

NOFL.id_note: Long, steady 'wick' series all on one pitch, plus a single loud 'klee-yer.' The even pitch separates it from the wilder Pileated.

RHWO.id_note: Harsh, raspy 'tchur' or 'queeah' — higher, sharper, and grittier than Red-bellied Woodpecker's rounder roll.
